title: Foundations
intro: Knife work, heat, seasoning and the mise en place that every French kitchen stands on. Learn these first, and every chapter after reads as a variation on them.

entries.title: Mise en place
entries.summary: Mise en place, everything in its place, is the work a cook does before the first ticket: ingredients prepared, tools set out and a plan in the head, so that service is spent cooking rather than searching.
entries.guest: Mise en place means everything in its place: a kitchen prepares every ingredient before the doors open, so each plate can be cooked the moment it is ordered.

paras: Mise en place (meez ahn PLAHS) is French for putting in place, and kitchens use it to mean everything in its place: every ingredient prepared, every tool at hand and a plan for the service ahead, all set before the first ticket arrives. A cook with good mise spends service cooking. A cook without it spends service hunting for a spoon while the hollandaise splits and the fish overcooks.

It matters because a rush leaves no time to think twice. Every minute spent peeling a shallot during service is a minute a plate waits under the lamp. Mise en place moves the slow, careful work into the quiet hours, so the busy hours run on speed and repetition.

Building a station starts with the board. Lay a damp cloth or a non-slip mat under it so it cannot slide, because a board that moves is how cooks cut themselves. Set the knives beside it, with two or three dry side towels folded at hand: a dry towel for lifting hot pans, never a wet one, which carries heat straight into the hand. Ninth pans, small steel inserts a ninth the size of a full hotel pan, hold the cut vegetables in a row within arm's reach, with salt, pepper and oils where the hand finds them without looking. Add a bowl for scraps and a sanitiser bucket with its cloth.

The prep list says what to make today; the par says how much. A par is the quantity of each item a station needs on hand for one service, set by the chef from the covers, the number of guests expected. Before setting up, a sauce cook reads the book, the reservation list, to see how many covers are booked, when the rush lands and whether a large party may order the same dish at once. The cook then counts what is left from yesterday, takes it from the par and makes the difference.

At a sauce station the mise is exact. Clarified butter sits warm, never hot, ready for hollandaise. The vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction for béarnaise is made and strained. Shallots are ciselé, cut into fine, even dice with a sharp knife so they are cut, not crushed. Herbs are picked, the leaves pulled from their stems. Stocks are hot at the back of the stove, so a pan sauce can be built in the minutes a steak rests.

Working clean as you go is part of the mise, not a chore after it. Wipe the board between jobs, sweep scraps into the scrap bowl rather than pushing them to the edge, and change a towel once it is wet. Every container that goes into the fridge carries a label: what it is, the date it was made, the cook's initials and the use-by date the kitchen sets. Under the FDA Food Code, most perishable ready-to-eat foods made in the kitchen and kept at 5°C (41°F) or colder must be used or thrown away within seven days, the day they were made counting as day one.

In the end mise en place is a habit of mind. The cook who has it thinks one step ahead of the ticket: while one plate cooks, the next pan is heating and the garnish for the third is in reach. Chefs read a cook's head from the state of the station.

Servers keep a mise of their own: pens, a crumber, a wine key, polished glasses and the notes from lineup, the short meeting before service where the day's food is explained. At Brennan's, which Gulf fish is running today is learned at lineup, and so are the varieties in Maggie's Mushrooms and how they are cooked. A server who reaches the table already knowing has good mise.

entries.title: Knife cuts
entries.summary: The classical knife cuts give every vegetable a named shape and size, from the tiny brunoise to the large dice, so that pieces cook evenly, look clean on the plate and yield the same every time.
entries.guest: Classically, vegetables are cut to one even size, so every piece cooks in the same time and softens together in the sauce.

paras: A knife cut is a shape and a size with a name. French kitchens fixed the names so that a chef can call for brunoise or julienne and every cook on the line cuts the same piece. Even cuts matter for three reasons. Pieces of one size cook in one time, so nothing stays raw while its neighbour turns to mush. They look clean, which shows in a clear sauce where every piece is visible. And they yield predictably: a cook who cuts evenly knows how many portions a case of onions will make.

Hold the knife in a pinch grip: the thumb and the side of the forefinger pinch the blade just ahead of the bolster, the thick join of blade and handle, and the other fingers wrap the handle. The guiding hand makes the claw: fingertips curled under, thumb tucked behind, so the flat of the blade rides against the knuckles. The knuckle is the guide. Move it back a little and the next slice is that much thicker, while the fingertips stay out of the way.

Square the vegetable first. Trim a carrot or potato into a neat block so it lies flat, cut planks of the thickness wanted, stack them, cut sticks, then cut the sticks across into dice. The trimmings go to stock or purée, not the bin.

The classical sizes run as a ladder. Julienne is a stick about 3 mm (1/8 inch) square and 5 to 6 cm (about 2 inches) long; cut across, it gives brunoise (broon-WAHZ), cubes about 3 mm (1/8 inch). Bâtonnet is a stick about 6 mm (1/4 inch) square and 6 cm (about 2 1/4 inches) long; cut across, it gives small dice. Medium dice is about 12 mm (1/2 inch) and large dice about 20 mm (3/4 inch). Schools vary a little; follow the recipe and the chef.

Some cuts are named for the job. To ciseler (seez-LAY) a shallot, halve it through the root, make thin lengthwise cuts towards the root without cutting through it, make one or two flat cuts parallel to the board, then slice down across the cuts into fine dice: the root holds it together, so it is cut, not crushed. Émincer (ay-man-SAY) is to slice thinly. Chiffonade (shif-uh-NAHD) is for leaves, stacked, rolled tight and sliced across into ribbons. Concassée (kohn-ka-SAY) is tomato peeled, seeded and chopped: score it, drop it into boiling water for 10 to 15 seconds, refresh it in iced water, slip off the skin, scoop out the seeds and chop.

Two cuts belong to the classical garnishes. Paysanne (pay-ee-ZAHN), country style, is thin tiles about 12 mm (1/2 inch) across and 3 mm (1/8 inch) thick, following the vegetable's shape, for soups. To tourner (toor-NAY) is to turn a potato or carrot into a small barrel with seven even faces, about 5 cm (2 inches) long: a slow test of a steady hand.

The holy trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, is classically cut to an even small dice so the three soften together in the fat; uneven pieces leave the small ones scorching while the large ones stay crunchy. At Brennan's it starts the Seafood Gumbo and the Turtle Soup, taught under The holy trinity; how fine the kitchen cuts it is a question for the chef.

A sharp knife is the careful knife. A dull edge needs force, slips off an onion's skin and goes where the cook never meant it to. Hone on a steel before each session and through the day: honing straightens the fine edge that bends with use. Sharpening on a whetstone grinds new metal into a fresh edge and is needed far less often. Keep the board on its damp cloth, never leave a knife in a sink of water, and carry it point down at your side, calling out as you pass.

On the floor, the cuts give a server words for what the guest sees: the tiny even cubes in a sauce are brunoise, the fine ribbons of herb are chiffonade. A guest who asks why the vegetables are all so soft and even hears the plain truth: they were cut to one size, so they cooked in one time. The names as they appear on a menu or ticket are taught under Cuts by name.

faults.fix: Hone the edge and slice with clean strokes; cut a chiffonade close to service so the leaves stay green.

entries.title: Heat and the pan
entries.say: As it reads: heat and the pan.
entries.summary: How heat travels into food, why browning needs a hot, dry surface, how the stove's heat ladder and each kind of pan behave, and how a cook reads heat with the ear, the eye, the nose and the probe.
entries.guest: The golden crust comes from a hot, dry pan: the surface browns quickly while the inside stays moist and tender.

paras: Every cooking method is a way of moving heat into food, and heat travels three ways. Conduction passes it by touch, from flame to pan to food, which is why a steak browns where it meets the metal. Convection carries it through a moving liquid or gas: oil in a fryer, water in a pot, the hot air of an oven. Radiation crosses open space, from the glowing salamander, the overhead grill above the line, or from coals beneath a grill.

Browning gives much of the flavour, through two reactions. The Maillard reaction joins proteins and sugars into hundreds of new flavours and a brown colour; it is slow at lower heat and quick from about 140°C (284°F), the crust on seared meat, toast and roasted coffee. Caramelisation is sugar alone breaking down at higher heat, from roughly 160 to 170°C (320 to 338°F) for table sugar, giving the sweet, bitter notes of caramel.

Water sets the limit. At sea level, as in New Orleans, water boils at 100°C (212°F), and food in water or steam cannot rise above that at its surface, far below browning heat. So a poached or boiled food never browns, and a wet steak, or a pan so crowded that the juices cannot evaporate, steams grey instead of searing. Dry the surface, heat the pan first and leave space between the pieces.

The heat ladder, in outline: low heat melts butter, softens vegetables without colour and keeps a sauce warm; medium heat cooks eggs and turns onions golden; high heat sears, browns and brings water to a fast boil. Tell a simmer from a boil by the bubbles. At a simmer, small bubbles rise lazily and break at the surface; at a boil, large bubbles roll without stopping and keep rolling when stirred.

Read heat with every sense. Food laid in a hot pan sizzles at once; silence means the pan was cold. Oil shimmers when it is hot enough to sauté and smokes when it starts to burn. Browning smells toasty; burning smells sharp and acrid. Then use the probe, an instant-read thermometer, in the thickest part and away from bone, checked in iced water, where it reads 0°C (32°F).

Heat does not stop when food leaves the pan. The outside is hotter than the centre and that stored heat keeps moving inwards, so a thick roast taken out at 52°C (126°F) in the centre may reach about 57°C (135°F) as it rests. Thick food carries over more than thin, so cooks take it off a little early and let it rest.

Pans each have a job. Heavy pans hold heat and spread it evenly, so they recover quickly when cold food goes in; thin pans heat and cool fast and form hot spots. Cast iron is slow to heat but holds it like a stone, for searing and blackening. Stainless steel bonded round an aluminium or copper core is the all-rounder: it does not react with acid, and it keeps the fond, the browned film a pan sauce is built on.

Copper answers the flame fastest and most evenly, lined with tin or steel because bare copper reacts with food. Non-stick is for eggs and delicate fish at moderate heat. Bare aluminium conducts well and costs little, but it reacts with acid: tomato, wine or lemon cooked in it can taste metallic, and a white sauce whisked in it can turn grey.

Blackening is cast iron at its limit: in the classic method, food is dipped in melted butter, coated in spice and laid in a dry cast-iron skillet heated past smoking, where butter and spice char to a dark crust in about two minutes a side for a fish fillet while the inside stays moist. It throws heavy smoke, so the hood runs on full. The Blackened Tofu uses the method, and Blackening has its own entry. Frying is convection in oil: at about 175 to 190°C (347 to 374°F) the coating browns fast while the inside steams, as on the Popcorn Shrimp, taught under Frying. Questions about butter, coatings, shared fryers or the oil go to the kitchen.
At the table, heat becomes the words for texture: a golden crust from a hot pan, tenderness from a slow simmer. Use them only for what tonight's dish truly is, as learned at lineup.

faults.fault: Grey, steamed meat with no crust
faults.cause: A wet surface, a pan not yet hot, or a pan so crowded that the juices pool.
faults.fix: Pat the food dry, heat the pan before the fat and food go in, and cook in batches with space between pieces.

The Popcorn Shrimp are fried in hot oil, convection at work: the coating browns and crisps while the shrimp steam inside. Questions about the coating, shared fryers or the oil go to the kitchen.

cards.front: What are the three ways heat reaches food?
cards.back: Conduction by touch through the pan, convection in moving oil, water or air, and radiation across space from a salamander or coals.

cards.front: What is a salamander, and how does it heat food?
cards.back: The overhead grill above the line; it cooks by radiation, glowing heat sent across open space onto the top of the food.

cards.front: What is the Maillard reaction?
cards.back: The browning of proteins and sugars together into new flavours and a brown colour, quick from about 140°C (284°F): the crust on seared meat and toast.

cards.front: How does caramelisation differ from the Maillard reaction?
cards.back: Caramelisation is sugar alone breaking down at higher heat, table sugar from roughly 160 to 170°C (320 to 338°F); Maillard needs protein as well as sugar.

cards.front: Why does a poached or boiled food never brown?
cards.back: Water cannot get hotter than 100°C (212°F) at sea level, well below the heat browning needs.

cards.front: Why does a crowded pan steam instead of searing?
cards.back: The pieces give off more juice than can evaporate, so they sit in liquid held near 100°C (212°F) and turn grey rather than brown.

cards.front: How do you tell a simmer from a boil?
cards.back: At a simmer, small bubbles rise lazily and break at the surface; at a boil, large bubbles roll constantly and keep rolling when stirred.

cards.front: What does a heavy pan do that a thin one cannot?
cards.back: It holds heat and spreads it evenly, so it recovers fast when cold food goes in; a thin pan reacts quickly and forms hot spots.

cards.front: Why not cook tomato or wine in bare aluminium?
cards.back: Bare aluminium reacts with acid, giving a metallic taste, and can turn a white sauce grey; use stainless steel or enamel instead.

cards.front: What is carryover heat in cooking?
cards.back: Heat stored in the outside of food keeps moving inwards after it leaves the heat, so food comes off a little early and rests.

cards.front: What do the sizzle, the shimmer and the smoke tell a cook about a pan?

entries.title: White stock
entries.say: As it reads: white stock, or fond blanc, fohn BLAHN.
entries.summary: Fond blanc, white stock, is chicken or veal bones simmered gently from cold water with a pale mirepoix and herbs, never roasted, for a clear, light, gelatinous liquid that becomes velouté, suprême, allemande and the white soups.
entries.guest: A velouté starts from white stock: chicken or veal bones simmered slowly for hours, which gives the sauce its body and a clean, savoury depth.

paras: White stock, fond blanc (fohn BLAHN) in French, is the pale stock of the classical kitchen: chicken or veal bones simmered slowly in water with vegetables and herbs, then strained. Nothing is browned. The bones are blanched or rinsed, never roasted, and the vegetables go in raw, so the stock stays pale, clear and light, tasting of the bones rather than of a roasting pan. Fond means base, and that is its job: it is a building block, not a soup.

A good white stock is judged cold. Its body is gelatine, drawn from the collagen in knuckles, joints, wings and feet by hours of gentle heat, and a stock with enough of it sets to a soft wobble in the fridge. That gelatine gives a sauce its silky feel and lets it reduce to a gloss.

Cut the bones to fit the pot: veal knuckles, or chicken carcasses, necks, wings and feet. For the clearest stock, blanch them: cover with cold water, bring to the boil, drain and rinse away the grey scum. Chicken bones are often only rinsed well, which keeps more flavour.

Cover the bones with cold water by about 5 cm (2 inches). Starting cold matters: as the water warms slowly, the proteins that would cloud the stock gather into scum and rise, where they can be skimmed. Bring it slowly to a bare simmer, around 85 to 90°C (185 to 194°F), the surface just trembling, and skim as the scum and fat gather. Never let it boil: boiling churns fat and protein back into the liquid and leaves it cloudy and greasy.

Once the first heavy scum is off, add the white mirepoix, onion, celery and leek in large pieces, with a bouquet garni of thyme, bay and parsley stalks tied in a leek leaf, and a few peppercorns. Some kitchens add a little carrot; the white mirepoix leaves it out for the palest stock. Simmer chicken about 3 to 5 hours and veal 6 to 8, topping up with cold water if the bones show. Add no salt: the stock will be reduced, and salt concentrates with it.
Ladle the stock out, rather than tipping the pot, through a chinois, the fine conical sieve, lined with muslin for the clearest result. Cool it fast, then lift off the fat once it has set on top.

A working proportion is about 4 kg (about 9 lb) of bones to 6 litres (about 6 quarts) of cold water and 500 g (1 lb) of white mirepoix, roughly one part vegetables to eight of bones by weight, for about 4 litres (about 1 gallon) of finished stock. More bones give a richer stock; more water gives a thin one that never sets.

White stock is the liquid of the velouté family. Thickened with a blond roux it becomes velouté; chicken velouté reduced with cream becomes suprême; veal velouté bound with egg yolks and sharpened with lemon becomes allemande (Escoffier's also took mushroom liquor and no cream; many kitchens today use a yolk and cream liaison). It makes the cream soups, poaches a chicken and cooks a blanquette, the veal stew in a white sauce. Escoffier began his Guide Culinaire (1903) with the stocks, the fonds de cuisine, before a single sauce.

Most faults come from heat and haste. A cloudy stock was boiled, stirred or left unskimmed; straining through damp muslin helps, though only a raft, taught under Clarifying, will make it fully clear again. A thin stock that will not set had too much water, too few joints or too little time: reduce it gently. A bitter edge comes from vegetables and peppercorns left in too long, or from scorching on the bottom of the pot.

Guests rarely see stock, but they meet it in every velouté, cream soup and white braise. A soup or sauce built on chicken or veal stock carries meat even when nothing on the plate looks like meat, so a guest who avoids meat, or eats vegetarian, gets the answer from the kitchen, never a guess from the server.

faults.fix: Chill it and lift off the set fat; keep the next batch below the boil.

faults.fix: Keep the heat low, keep the bones covered and strain the stock as soon as it is done.

questions.q: How do you know a white stock has plenty of gelatine?
questions.answer: It sets to a soft wobble when cold
distractors: It stays runny in the fridge

entries.title: Brown stock
entries.say: As it reads: brown stock, or fond brun, fohn BRUHN.
entries.summary: Veal or beef bones roasted deep brown with onion, carrot, celery and tomato purée, then simmered for hours in cold water, unsalted. Full of gelatine, it is the base of espagnole, demi-glace, glace de viande and every classical brown sauce.
entries.guest: Brown stock is roasted bones and vegetables simmered for hours: you never see it on the plate, but it gives the classic dark sauces their depth.

paras: Brown stock, fond brun in French, is made by roasting bones until they are deep brown, then simmering them slowly in water with vegetables. Fond means base, and that is its job: nobody eats it as it is, but almost every dark sauce on a classical menu starts here. Roasting gives colour and a toasty depth; the long simmer melts the collagen in the bones into gelatine, which gives the stock body and sets it to a soft jelly when cold.

Veal bones are the classical choice, knuckles and neck above all: young bones carry plenty of collagen and a mild flavour that takes on whatever the sauce adds later. Beef bones give a darker, beefier stock with less body, and many kitchens use both. The vegetables are a mirepoix of onion, carrot and celery, cut large.

Roast the bones in one layer at about 220°C (428°F) for 45 minutes to an hour, turning once or twice, until they are a deep, even mahogany, never black. Add the mirepoix for the last 20 to 30 minutes so it browns too. Then smear tomato purée, the thick concentrate called tomato paste in American kitchens, over everything and roast a few minutes more, until it turns from bright red to rust. This is the pincé: it adds colour and sweetness and cooks off the raw tomato taste.

Lift everything into the stockpot and pour the fat from the tray. Set the tray over the heat, add a little water or wine and scrape up the browned juices stuck to it, then tip them into the pot. That is deglazing: those juices carry much of the flavour.

Cover the bones with cold water, bring it up slowly and skim the grey foam as it rises. Hold it at a bare simmer, about 85 to 90°C (185 to 194°F), a bubble breaking only now and then, for 8 to 12 hours, skimming fat and foam through the day. Add parsley stalks, thyme, bay and a few peppercorns for the last hour. Never add salt. Strain through a chinois, the fine conical strainer, without pressing, cool it quickly and lift off the set fat.

A dependable batch: 4.5 kg (10 lb) of bones, 450 g (1 lb) of mirepoix, 115 g (4 oz) of tomato purée and 5.7 litres (6 quarts) of cold water, for roughly 3.8 litres (1 gallon) of stock. The mirepoix is about a tenth of the bone weight, two parts onion to one each of carrot and celery. The water covers the bones by a few centimetres; more only thins the stock.

Brown stock is the root of the brown family. Thickened with a brown roux and simmered with mirepoix and tomato, it becomes espagnole. Espagnole reduced with more brown stock becomes demi-glace, the base of bordelaise, chasseur, Robert and many more. Reduced alone until syrupy, brown stock becomes glace de viande; simmered with the juices of a roast, it makes a jus. Each has its own entry, and a sauce is only as good as the stock beneath it.

Burnt bones make a bitter stock that no skimming will rescue: roast to deep brown and stop. A stock left to boil churns fat and fine particles into the liquid, so it turns cloudy and greasy. Too much tomato makes it sour and red rather than brown, and pale bones give a weak, grey one. Salt cannot be undone: a stock may be reduced to a tenth of its volume and every grain of salt stays behind.

A guest never orders brown stock, but a server describes it every night inside the brown sauces. At Brennan's, the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen belongs to this family. Classically it is shallots and red wine reduced with brown stock or demi-glace; the New Orleans version adds onion, garlic, often ham and mushroom, beef stock and red wine, frequently bound with a roux. The house's own words are a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce. Whether tonight's carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef, never a guess.

Covered in a hot oven for 1 hour

entries.title: Fumet de poisson
entries.summary: A quick stock of lean white fish bones sweated in butter with aromatics, wetted with white wine and cold water and simmered for only 20 to 30 minutes. It is the base of fish velouté, the white wine sauces and the poaching liquor for fish.
entries.guest: A fumet is a light stock made from the bones of white fish, white wine and herbs. It gives a fish sauce its clean taste of the sea.

paras: Fumet de poisson is fish stock made fast. Fumet means scent, and a good one smells of the sea and of white wine, never of old fish. Where a veal stock simmers all day, a fumet is done in half an hour: fish bones are small and soft and give up their flavour and gelatine quickly, and left longer they give up bitterness instead. It is the white base of the fish kitchen, under the sauces for sole, flounder or redfish and in the liquid fish is poached in.

Cooks draw a loose line between a plain fish stock, bones simmered in water, and a fumet, where the bones are first sweated in butter and part of the liquid is white wine, which gives a fuller, rounder taste. Many kitchens use the two words for the same thing.

Use the frames and heads of lean white fish: sole, flounder, snapper, sheepshead, and redfish and the other drums. Their bones are rich in gelatine and mild in taste. Oily fish such as salmon, mackerel or bluefish make a strong, greasy stock that tastes fishy in a sauce, so keep them out. The frames should be fresh, with clear eyes and a clean smell of the sea.
Pull out the gills, which are bitter and full of blood, chop the frames and soak them in cold water for about 20 minutes, until it runs clear. Blood left on the bones turns the stock grey and strong.

Melt butter in a wide pan and add sliced onion or shallot, celery or leek white, and mushroom trimmings, which add savour and keep the stock pale. Lay the bones on top, cover with a lid or a circle of paper and sweat them gently for about 5 minutes, without colour, until the scraps of flesh turn white. Pour in dry white wine and let it bubble for a minute, then add cold water just to cover.

Bring it to a bare simmer, skim, and add parsley stalks, a bay leaf, thyme and a few white peppercorns. Simmer for 20 to 30 minutes and no longer. Ladle it gently through a fine strainer lined with muslin, without pressing the bones, which would cloud it, then cool it quickly.

A working batch: 1.5 to 2 kg (3 to 4 lb) of bones, about 300 g (11 oz) of aromatics and mushroom trim, 250 ml (1 cup) of dry white wine and 2 litres (about 2 quarts) of cold water, for roughly 2 litres of fumet. Cover the bones only just: extra water makes a thin stock, and longer simmering only adds bitterness.

Thickened with a blond roux, fumet becomes fish velouté, the parent of the white fish sauces: sauce vin blanc, normande and Bercy among them, each taught under The velouté family. Fumet is also the classic liquor for poaching fish, reduced afterwards into that plate's sauce, and reduced on its own it becomes glace de poisson.

The Louisiana cousin is a stock of shrimp heads and shells, crab bodies or crawfish shells. The shells are toasted in a little fat until red and sweet smelling, then simmered with onion, celery and bay for 30 to 45 minutes, and a seafood gumbo is built on it. Brennan's own guide says a seafood gumbo uses a stock made from the seafood shells, and the house's published gumbo recipe uses crab stock; whether the dining room gumbo follows it is confirmed at lineup. Keep shell stocks labelled apart from fish stock, because when a guest asks about shellfish the answer comes from the kitchen.

A bitter fumet simmered too long or kept its gills. A grey or murky one carried blood that was never soaked out, was boiled, or was pressed through the strainer. A greasy, fishy one was made with oily fish or stale bones. None of these can be fixed in the pot: start again with fresh, lean bones and a timer.

The word fumet rarely reaches a menu, but a guest meets it in the white fish sauces. A server can say the sauce is built on a light stock of fish bones, white wine and herbs. What went into a sauce, fish or shell stock included, is a question for the kitchen.

entries.title: Court-bouillon and nage
entries.summary: A court-bouillon is a short broth of water, an acid, aromatics and salt, simmered briefly to flavour and poach fish and seafood. Refined, reduced and mounted with butter, it becomes a nage, a broth fine enough to serve.
entries.guest: À la nage means the seafood arrives swimming in its own light broth of white wine, vegetables and herbs, so the broth is the sauce.

paras: Court-bouillon means short broth: short because it cooks briefly, 20 to 30 minutes in most kitchens today and about an hour in Escoffier's vinegar version, against the many hours of a stock. It is water sharpened with an acid, white wine, vinegar or lemon, with sliced onion, carrot, celery, herbs and salt. Unlike a stock, it is not a base to be reduced into sauces. It has two jobs: to flavour what cooks in it, and to be the poaching liquid itself, for whole fish, fish steaks, crawfish, shrimp, crab and lobster, and for sweetbreads, the glands of veal or lamb.

The acid helps the proteins on the surface of the fish set, so the flesh holds together, and it keeps white flesh white. The salt seasons the food right through, which is why a court-bouillon is salted where a stock never is: it will not be reduced, so the salt is never concentrated.

Bring the water, acid, vegetables, a bouquet garni and salt to the boil, then simmer for 20 to 30 minutes, adding a few peppercorns only for the last 10, since they turn bitter if simmered long. Strain it, or leave the vegetables in for a rustic dish.

Once the food goes in, the liquid is never boiled again. Hold it just below a simmer, about 75 to 85°C (167 to 185°F), the surface barely trembling. A whole fish starts in cool court-bouillon and is brought up gently, so the outside does not overcook and split before the heat reaches the bone. Fillets, portions and shrimp go into liquid that is already hot, because they are thin enough to cook through before the outside toughens.

A working court-bouillon is 2 litres (about 2 quarts) of water to 250 ml (1 cup) of dry white wine, or about 100 ml of white wine vinegar, with a sliced onion and carrot, a stick of celery, a bouquet garni and about 20 g of salt, roughly 1 per cent. Escoffier varied the court-bouillon with the fish: his vinegar court-bouillon was for salmon and trout, whole or in large cuts, and salted water with milk and slices of lemon was for turbot and brill, to keep the flesh white.

A nage, from à la nage, swimming, is a court-bouillon made fine enough to serve. The vegetables are cut neatly, often thin rounds of carrot and shallot; the broth is strained and reduced to concentrate it, and cold butter is often whisked in at the end, monter au beurre, so it turns glossy and rounder without thickening into a coating sauce. Scallops, lobster or langoustines poached in it come to the table swimming in it, so the broth is the sauce.

The Louisiana seafood boil is a court-bouillon taken to the limit. A big pot of water is loaded with salt, cayenne, lemon halves, onions, garlic and bay and brought to a hard boil. Crawfish, crab or shrimp go in with potatoes and corn. Crawfish boil for only a few minutes; then the fire goes off and they soak, often 15 to 30 minutes, drinking in the seasoning as the pot cools. Here the boil is deliberate, and it is the soak that carries the flavour.

Boiling is the commonest fault: it breaks fish apart, toughens shrimp and clouds the broth. Used before it has simmered, it tastes of little but sour water. A whole fish dropped into fierce heat splits its skin and overcooks outside while the centre stays raw.

New Orleans uses the same word for something quite different. The Creole courtbouillon, usually written as one word and said coo-bee-YON in Louisiana, is a thick stew of redfish in a roux-based tomato sauce with the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, served over rice. It shares the French name and little else, and has its own entry, Courtbouillon.

On a menu, à la nage tells the guest the dish comes in a light broth meant to be spooned up, so set a spoon and offer bread. Describe it as seafood poached in a light broth of white wine, vegetables and herbs, and served in it. Questions about what went into the broth go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Glace de viande and the glaces
entries.summary: A glace is stock reduced slowly until syrupy, setting firm when cold: glace de viande from brown stock, glace de volaille from chicken, glace de poisson from fish. A spoonful deepens a sauce; it is the concentrated end of the stockpot.
entries.guest: Glace de viande is brown stock cooked down to a rich, glossy glaze. A little whisked into a sauce, as in the sauce Foyot, gives it deep, savoury flavour.

paras: A glace, French for glaze, is stock reduced until only a small fraction remains: thick enough to coat a spoon like syrup while warm, and firm as rubber when cold. Glace de viande, meat glaze, comes from brown stock; glace de volaille from white chicken stock; glace de poisson from fish fumet. Nothing is added to thicken it. Its body is the gelatine of the bones, concentrated along with the flavour, so a glace is only as good as the stock it began as.

It is used by the spoonful, not the ladle. A teaspoon stirred into a pan sauce gives depth, colour and gloss that would otherwise take hours, and a block in the fridge holds the flavour of a whole stockpot. Between stock and glace sits demi-glace, half glaze, which has its own entry.

Start with a large batch of well-skimmed, unsalted stock in a wide pot at a steady simmer, and keep skimming: the reduction concentrates any fat or scum along with the flavour. Each time the volume halves, strain it through a fine chinois into a smaller, clean pan. That leaves the sediment behind and keeps the liquid deep enough that the sides and bottom do not scorch. Lower the heat as it thickens. The first litres go quickly; the last stage is slow and needs a watchful eye, because a glace that catches turns bitter in moments.
It is ready when it coats the back of a spoon thickly, the bubbles turn large and glossy, and a drop on a cold plate sets almost at once. Pour it into a shallow tray or small moulds and chill it.

Roughly 8 to 10 litres (about 2 to 2.6 gallons) of stock reduce to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of glace, a loss of nine tenths or more, over several hours. That is why the stock must be unsalted: a stock seasoned to taste would make a glace ten times too salty.

Glace de viande finishes brown pan sauces and makes sauce Foyot, which is béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in; Foyot has its own entry beside Choron. A pale glace does the same work for white sauces: a few spoonfuls stirred into suprême, the cream-enriched chicken velouté, give sauce ivoire, named for its ivory colour. Glace de poisson strengthens a thin fish sauce, and melted glace brushed over a roast or braise gives it shine.

Jus is the lighter road. A jus is the juice of a roast: the pan is deglazed, the juices simmered with a little stock, skimmed of fat, strained and served thin and clear. A jus lié is the same juice lightly thickened with arrowroot or cornflour slaked in cold water, that is, mixed smooth with it first, just enough to coat a spoon. Since the nouvelle cuisine of the 1970s, many kitchens have preferred jus and reduced stocks to flour-thickened brown sauces.

Salt and scorching are the two enemies. Only an unsalted stock makes a usable glace, and in the last stage, with almost no water left, the glace catches on a hot pan in moments and turns dark and bitter: lower the heat, move it to a smaller pan and stir. A cloudy, greasy glace came from stock that was not skimmed or strained well, and one that will not set began as a thin stock.

At Brennan's, a server meets glace de viande in the sauce Foyot (fwah-YO) on the Roasted Chateaubriand. The house guide describes Foyot as béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in: a spoonful turns pale, sharp béarnaise tawny, deeper and more savoury. That matters on this plate, because tenderloin is one of the leanest, mildest cuts on the animal, and the sauce brings the depth the meat lacks. Say it as béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze, and send any question about what is in it to the kitchen.

Glace keeps chilled as a block to cut from, or set in small portions so a cook takes only what a sauce needs, labelled and dated like every stock, and frozen for longer keeping. At the table, a server calls it a rich reduction of stock that gives a sauce its depth.

entries.title: Roux
entries.summary: Flour cooked in fat in equal weights, then whisked into a liquid and simmered to thicken it. The classical binder of French sauces: cooked white for béchamel, blond for velouté and brown for espagnole, and taken far darker in Louisiana.
entries.guest: A roux is flour cooked slowly in fat, the base that thickens many classic sauces and soups. It is part of why a gumbo or a turtle soup tastes deep rather than brothy.

paras: A roux, said ROO, is flour cooked in fat and then used to thicken a liquid. The fat coats each grain of flour, so when hot stock or milk goes in, the starch swells evenly instead of clumping. Cooking the flour first also takes away its raw, pasty taste and, the longer it goes, adds colour and a toasted flavour. It is the classical thickener of French sauces: béchamel, velouté and espagnole all stand on it.

French cooks name a roux by its colour. A white roux is cooked only until the raw flour smell goes, with no colour at all, for béchamel. A blond roux goes on to pale straw, for velouté. A brown roux is cooked slowly to a light nut brown that smells of toast, for espagnole and the brown sauces. Louisiana cooks keep going, to peanut butter, chocolate and brick, a ladder with its own entry.

For a French roux, use clarified butter: butter with its water and milk solids taken off, so it cooks longer without scorching. In Louisiana the fat is usually oil or lard, which stand the long heat of a dark roux. Melt the fat in a heavy pan over a low to moderate heat, add the same weight of flour and stir it into a smooth paste, like wet sand, reaching into the corners. A white roux takes 2 to 3 minutes, a blond about 5 and a brown 10 to 15 or more: read the colour and the smell, not the clock.

Then the temperature rule: cool roux into hot liquid, or hot roux into cool liquid. The contrast lets the starch disperse before it swells; hot into hot spits and lumps. Whisk the liquid in a ladle at a time, smoothing each addition before the next. Bring it to the boil, whisking, because flour reaches its full thickness near 95°C (203°F), then lower it to a gentle simmer and cook it out for at least 15 to 20 minutes, until no floury taste is left.

Weigh equal amounts of fat and flour. For a medium sauce that coats a spoon, use about 50 to 70 g (about 2 oz) each of butter and flour for 1 litre (about 1 quart) of liquid. Use about half that for a thin sauce or soup, and half as much again for a thick, binding one: the Table's béchamel recipe, made to bind gratins and lasagne, runs thick, at 50 g of each to 600 ml (about 2 1/2 cups) of milk.

Thickening power falls as the colour deepens. Long heat breaks some of the starch into shorter pieces that brown and taste toasty but can no longer swell and bind. Weight for weight, a brown roux thickens less than a white one, so espagnole takes more of it, and a dark Louisiana roux flavours far more than it thickens.

Lumps mean the liquid went in too fast or at the wrong temperature: whisk hard as the sauce comes to the boil and strain out what remains. A pasty taste means the sauce was not cooked out, so give it more time. Black flecks and a sharp smell mean the roux has burnt, and there is no rescue: start again.

Roux is French for russet, a reddish brown. Flour cooked in lard appears in La Varenne's Le Cuisinier françois of 1651 as a liaison de farine, a flour binder, and by the end of that century cooks were calling it farine frite, fried flour, or roux. It took over from much of the bread that had thickened older sauces.

At Brennan's, roux links three signatures. The Seafood Gumbo and the Turtle Soup both stand on a well-browned roux, and the house's published gumbo recipe starts with a dark mahogany roux; confirm at lineup that the dining room gumbo follows it. New Orleans marchand de vin, the red wine sauce on the Eggs Hussarde, is often roux-bound too. How dark the kitchen takes each one is the chef's call.

At the table, describe a roux as flour slowly toasted in fat. Flour means wheat, so a roux-bound sauce or soup belongs in every allergen conversation, and each such question goes to the kitchen, never to a guess.

Roux is part of why the Turtle Soup tastes deep rather than brothy: Creole turtle soup is built on a brown roux with the trinity and tomato. How dark our kitchen takes it is a question for the chef.

entries.title: Beurre manié, slurries and liaisons
entries.say: As it reads: slurries and liaisons, with beurre manié, burr mahn-YAY.
entries.summary: The thickeners beyond roux: beurre manié kneaded from butter and flour, starch slurries of cornflour or arrowroot, the egg yolk and cream liaison, reduction, and the old binders. Each is chosen for flavour, clarity, holding time and what the guest can eat.
entries.guest: Some sauces are thickened at the last moment, with butter kneaded with flour, a little starch, or egg yolk and cream. The kitchen can tell you what binds each one.

paras: A roux is built in at the start. The thickeners here mostly come at the end, when a cook needs to tighten a braise, give body to a pan sauce or enrich a soup without starting again. They fall into four groups: flour held in butter, the beurre manié; pure starch mixed with cold liquid, the slurry; protein, the egg yolk and cream liaison; and water driven off, reduction. A good cook knows all four and chooses by what the dish and the guest need.

Beurre manié, kneaded butter, is equal weights of soft butter and flour worked into a paste; the butter coats the flour so it disperses without lumps. Whisk it into a simmering liquid a small piece at a time, letting each thicken before adding more, then simmer for 2 to 3 minutes to cook off the raw flour taste. It is the classic last-minute fix for a braise or stew that came out thin.

A slurry is a starch slaked, mixed smooth, in a little cold liquid, then stirred into a simmering one; dry starch in hot liquid seizes into lumps. Arrowroot thickens below the boil and stays clear and glossy, so it suits fruit sauces and glazes, but it turns slimy with milk or cream and thins if boiled long. Cornflour, cornstarch in America, must reach the boil to thicken fully; it clouds a sauce slightly and can thin and weep on long holding.

A liaison binds with egg yolk and cream. Whisk them together, then temper them: whisk in a ladle or two of the hot sauce to warm the yolks gently, and only then stir the mixture back into the pot, off the boil. Heat it gently, stirring, until it coats a spoon, and never let it boil, or the yolks curdle into grains.

It finishes a blanquette, veal in a creamy white sauce, and in many modern kitchens binds velouté into allemande, which Escoffier bound with yolks and no cream. In a sauce already bound with roux, the flour protects the yolks, which is why Escoffier could reduce allemande over a brisk fire; in a sauce with no flour, the no-boil rule is absolute.

Reduction thickens by driving off water. A sauce simmered uncovered concentrates, flavour, gelatine and salt alike, until it coats a spoon. It adds nothing, but it costs volume and time, so season after. How far to take it belongs to finishing a sauce.

About 30 g (1 oz) of beurre manié lightly thickens 500 ml (about 2 cups) of liquid. For a slurry, 1 tbsp (8 g) of cornflour slaked in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of cold water gives 250 ml (1 cup) of liquid a light coating body. A liaison is roughly three parts cream to one part yolk by volume: 3 yolks, about 50 ml, with 150 ml of cream for 1 litre (about 1 quart) of sauce, held below a simmer, around 80°C (176°F).

Older binders still have their place. A civet, a stew of hare or game, is finished with the animal's blood, stirred in at the end and never boiled. A purée of the vegetables cooked in the dish, or of potato or rice, thickens without flour. Bread, soaked or crumbed, binds a gazpacho or a rouille. In Louisiana, okra and filé, ground sassafras leaves, thicken gumbo, and have their own entry.

Choose a thickener by four things. Flavour: beurre manié tastes of butter and wheat, a liaison of egg and cream, arrowroot of almost nothing. Clarity: arrowroot stays clear, cornflour clouds a little, flour more. Holding: a liaison cannot be reboiled and cornflour thins with time, while roux holds best. And what the guest can eat: flour means wheat, a liaison means egg and cream, so any allergy question about a sauce goes to the kitchen.

entries.title: Clarifying: the consommé raft
entries.say: As it reads: clarifying, and consommé, kohn-so-MAY.
entries.summary: Consommé is a rich stock cleared to crystal brightness by a raft of minced lean meat, egg whites, mirepoix and tomato, which rises, sets and filters the stock as it barely simmers: the patient cook's test, and the clear soup of the old menus.
entries.guest: Consommé is a crystal-clear, deeply flavoured broth, cleared slowly and served very hot, plain in a cup or with a fine garnish. It is light in body but rich in taste.

paras: A consommé is a stock that has been clarified: made so clear you could read through it, deeper in flavour and amber in colour. Clarity comes from a raft, a mixture of minced lean meat, ground meat in American kitchens, egg whites, finely chopped mirepoix and tomato. As the stock heats, the proteins in the meat and whites set and rise, trapping the fine particles that cloud it, while the meat and vegetables add flavour of their own. A great consommé is crystal clear, amber to deep gold and full in taste, with a light body from gelatine that coats the lips but never feels thick.

Start with a cold, well-flavoured stock, fully skimmed of fat, white or brown as the soup needs. Mix the raft in a tall, heavy pot, whisk in the cold stock and set it over a moderate heat. Stir gently and often, scraping the bottom so nothing catches, as the temperature climbs slowly. Once the liquid turns thick and cloudy and the raft begins to gather, around 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F), stop stirring for good. The raft rises and binds into a firm cap.

Open a vent: with a ladle, make a hole near the edge of the raft so the stock can bubble up through it and baste the top. Lower the heat until the stock barely simmers, about 82 to 90°C (180 to 194°F), a lazy bubble through the vent, never a boil, for an hour to an hour and a half. A boil breaks the raft and churns everything back into the liquid.

To finish, ladle the consommé out through the vent without breaking the raft, and pass it through a sieve lined with damp muslin, the fine cotton cloth called cheesecloth in America. Then lift every trace of fat, by dragging strips of kitchen paper across the surface or by chilling it and lifting the set fat. Season lightly at the end.

A working raft for 4 litres (about 4 quarts) of stock is about 600 to 700 g (about 1 1/2 lb) of lean minced meat to match the stock, 6 to 8 egg whites, 450 g (1 lb) of finely chopped mirepoix and one or two chopped tomatoes. The meat must be lean, because fat clouds the result. A double consommé is made stronger again, usually with twice the meat in the raft, for a deeper flavour and colour.

A raft that will not form went into warm stock, was stirred too long or was short of protein; one that sinks or breaks was boiled or knocked. A cloudy consommé was boiled, stirred after the raft set or carried fat from the stock, and the cure is a fresh raft from cold. A pale one gains colour next time from an oignon brûlé, half an onion charred black on its cut face, added to the raft.

The old menus named a consommé by its garnish. Consommé brunoise carries a tiny dice of vegetables, about 3 mm, softened in butter. Consommé royale carries royale, a savoury custard of egg and consommé, gently poached, cooled and cut into small shapes. Consommé en tasse is served plain in a two-handled cup, to be sipped.

Fish has its own consommé, cleared with a raft of minced lean white fish and egg whites and simmered for only 30 to 45 minutes. Many kitchens now clear a gelatinous stock without a raft: frozen, then thawed slowly in the fridge over muslin, it drips through clear while the gelatine holds the cloud back, lighter in body and costing no meat.

Consommé belongs to the classical kitchen, and in London the celebrated turtle soup, made from green turtle shipped from the West Indies, was famously served clear, as a consommé, its body coming from the turtle's own gelatine, though thick versions were served too. New Orleans took turtle soup the other way: Creole cooks built it on a brown roux, the trinity and tomato into a thick, dark soup, finished with sherry and egg. The Creole soup has its own entry.

Present a consommé as a clear, concentrated broth, light in body but deep in flavour, and name its garnish plainly. Few menus carry one now, but its clarity is the lesson behind every stock and sauce: patience, a low heat and a clean pot.

cards.front: What is a consommé?
cards.back: A rich stock clarified by a raft of lean meat, egg white, mirepoix and tomato until it is crystal clear, amber and deeply flavoured.

cards.front: What goes into a consommé raft?
cards.back: Minced lean meat to match the stock, egg whites, finely chopped mirepoix and tomato, mixed together and whisked into cold stock.

cards.front: How does a raft clear a stock?
cards.back: As the stock heats, the proteins in the meat and whites set and rise, trapping the fine particles that cloud it.

cards.front: Why must the stock be cold when the raft goes in?
cards.back: Heated slowly from cold, the proteins gather the particles as they set; dropped into hot stock they set at once and trap little.

cards.front: When do you stop stirring the raft and stock?
cards.back: When the liquid turns thick and cloudy and the raft begins to gather, around 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F); stirring after that breaks the raft.

cards.front: What is the vent, and why make one?
cards.back: A hole opened near the edge of the raft so the stock bubbles gently through and bastes it, and so the consommé can be ladled out cleanly.

cards.front: Why must a consommé never boil?
cards.back: A boil breaks the raft and churns the trapped particles and fat back into the liquid, clouding it.

cards.front: How is a consommé finished after the simmer?
cards.back: Ladled out through the vent, passed through damp muslin, and every trace of fat lifted with kitchen paper or by chilling.

cards.front: What are the marks of a great consommé?
cards.back: Crystal clear, amber in colour, deep in flavour, with a light body from gelatine that coats the lips without feeling thick.

cards.front: What is a double consommé?
cards.back: A consommé made stronger again, usually with twice the meat in the raft, for a deeper flavour and colour.

cards.front: What are consommé brunoise, royale and en tasse?
cards.back: Brunoise carries a tiny vegetable dice; royale carries small shapes of savoury egg custard; en tasse is served plain in a cup.

cards.front: How did the old London turtle soup differ from the Creole one?
cards.back: London's banquet turtle soup was famously served clear, as a consommé, though thick versions were served too; Creole cooks made theirs thick and dark with a brown roux, the trinity and tomato.

questions.q: What does a classic consommé raft contain?
questions.answer: Lean minced meat, egg whites, mirepoix and tomato
distractors: Egg yolks, cream, minced shallot and lemon
Roasted bones, tomato purée, carrot and leek
Fatty minced pork, flour, onion and wine
questions.why: The meat and egg white proteins set and trap the cloud; the mirepoix and tomato add flavour and a little acidity.

questions.q: How does the raft clear the stock?
questions.answer: Its proteins set and trap the cloud
distractors: It thickens the stock until it sets
Its acid dissolves the cloudiness
It cools the stock below the boil
questions.why: As the stock warms, meat and egg white proteins coagulate and rise, carrying the particles that cloud a stock with them.

questions.q: At about what point do you stop stirring the raft and stock?
distractors: Never: stir until it is strained
At a rolling boil, 100°C (212°F)
Before the pot goes on the heat
questions.why: Stirring keeps the raft from catching while it warms; once it gathers, any stirring breaks it and clouds the stock.

questions.q: What is the vent in a consommé raft for?
questions.answer: So the stock bubbles up and bastes the raft
distractors: So steam escapes and the pot can boil hard
So more egg white can be added later
So cold stock can be topped up through it
questions.why: Through the vent the stock simmers gently against the raft, which keeps filtering it, and the consommé is ladled out there.

questions.q: A consommé was left at a rolling boil. What is the likely result?
questions.answer: A broken raft and a cloudy consommé
distractors: A clearer, brighter consommé
A thicker consommé, richer in gelatine
No change at all
questions.why: A boil tears the raft apart and churns the trapped particles and fat back into the liquid.

questions.q: What lines the sieve when a consommé is strained?
distractors: Baking parchment
A layer of flour
Nothing at all
questions.why: Damp muslin catches the finest particles the raft let through, and ladling through the vent keeps the raft whole.

questions.q: What makes a consommé a double consommé?
questions.answer: A raft with about twice the meat
distractors: Clarifying it twice with egg yolks
Serving it with a double garnish
Simmering it twice as long
questions.why: More meat in the raft adds more flavour and colour to a stock that is already strong.

questions.q: What is the garnish in a consommé royale?
questions.answer: Small shapes of savoury egg custard
distractors: A fine dice of vegetables
Nothing: it is served plain
Croutons fried in butter
questions.why: Royale is egg and consommé poached into a custard and cut into shapes; brunoise is the vegetable dice, and en tasse comes plain.

questions.q: Which turtle soup was famously served clear, as a consommé?
distractors: The Creole turtle soup
A turtle stew bound with filé
A gumbo with turtle and okra
questions.why: London's banquet turtle soup was famous in the classical clear style; New Orleans built its soup thick and dark on a brown roux and the trinity.

entries.title: Seasoning and tasting
entries.say: As it reads: seasoning and tasting.
entries.summary: Seasoning is the cook's constant job: salt, acid, pepper and heat added and adjusted by tasting, with a clean spoon every time. Salt early in a braise and late in a reduction, and taste the plate as a whole.
entries.guest: Our Creole spice is warm and savoury rather than fiery. If you would like a dish milder or with more heat, I will ask the kitchen what they can do.

paras: Seasoning means bringing a dish to its fullest flavour, with salt above all and with acid, pepper and heat. It is not a step at the end of a recipe but a habit through all of it: a cook tastes a sauce when it starts, as it reduces and before it leaves the pass. In the right amount, salt does more than make food salty: it sharpens the other flavours, softens bitterness and makes a dish taste more of itself. The palate that judges it is trained by tasting everything, every time.

Taste with a clean spoon each time, and never put a used spoon back into the pot. Stations keep clean tasting spoons in one container and used ones in another; the FDA Food Code, which most American health departments build their rules on, allows a utensil to taste food only once.

When to salt depends on what happens next. Salt a braise, a soup or a pot of beans early and lightly, so the salt works into the meat and vegetables, then adjust at the end. Salt a reduction late: as water boils away, everything left behind concentrates, salt included, so a sauce seasoned well at the start ends too salty. That is why stocks are never salted.

Acid is seasoning too. A drop of lemon juice or vinegar lifts a rich butter sauce, and a splash at the end wakes up a long-cooked gumbo or stew. Add it a few drops at a time and taste: the dish should taste brighter, not sour.

In Creole cooking, cayenne, black and white pepper and hot sauce are seasonings, there to warm and round a dish, not to dare the guest. White pepper leaves no dark specks in a pale sauce, black pepper brings aroma, cayenne a clean warmth that grows as a sauce reduces, and hot sauce vinegar as well as heat.

Finally, season the plate as a whole. Taste sauce, protein and garnish together in one forkful, the way the guest will: a sauce that seems strong on the spoon may be right over plain fish, and salty parts add up.

Correct a fault by what it calls for. Too salty: salt cannot be taken out, and a potato in the pot does little, so dilute with more of the unsalted base; acid or fat can soften the edge. Flat: salt first, then a drop of acid. Too sharp: butter, cream or a pinch of sugar. Too sweet: acid and salt, or a little heat. Too hot: more of the base, or fat, cream or starch to soften it, though nothing removes it.

At Brennan's, the house makes its own Creole spice, and the menu names it on the dinner Creole Hanger Steak; the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at breakfast and lunch is seasoned in the same style, and the two are different plates. The blend is not printed, so describe it as warm and savoury rather than fiery. The aged sherry that finishes the Turtle Soup seasons it the way lemon lifts fish: its acidity and nutty aroma cut the richness. Tell any guest who avoids alcohol that the sherry is there and never promise that it cooks off; whether it goes in at the kitchen, the pass or the table is a lineup question.

Describe heat honestly. Use the kitchen's own words, such as mild or mild to moderate, which is how the house notes describe the breakfast hanger and the Seafood Gumbo, and never promise a dish is not spicy when it carries cayenne. For a guest who wants less heat or more, or who asks about a particular spice, ask the kitchen what can be done rather than promising it.

faults.cause: Salted early in something that then reduced, or a heavy hand.
faults.fix: Dilute with more of the unsalted base, stock, cream or the main ingredient; acid or fat softens the edge, but nothing takes salt out.

faults.cause: Under-seasoned, most often short of salt.
faults.fix: Salt first, then a drop of lemon or vinegar, tasting after each.

faults.cause: Too much acid from lemon, vinegar, wine or tomato.
faults.fix: Round it with butter, cream or a pinch of sugar, or dilute it with more of the base.

faults.cause: Sweet vegetables, fruit or a heavy reduction.
faults.fix: Lift it with acid and salt, or a touch of heat.

faults.cause: Too much cayenne, pepper or hot sauce.
faults.fix: Dilute with more of the base, or soften with fat, cream or starch; for a guest's plate, the kitchen makes it again.

brennans.how: Brennan's makes its own Creole spice, named on the dinner hanger steak, and this breakfast and lunch hanger is seasoned in the same style. The blend is not printed, so describe it as warm and savoury rather than fiery, and take spice or heat questions to the kitchen.

Aged sherry finishes the Turtle Soup and seasons it the way lemon lifts fish: its acidity and nutty aroma cut the richness. Guests who avoid alcohol are told it is there; where it goes in is a lineup question.

cards.front: What is the rule for tasting spoons?
cards.back: A clean spoon for every taste and never back into the pot: the FDA Food Code lets a utensil taste food only once.

cards.front: What does salt do for a dish beyond making it salty?
cards.back: In the right amount it sharpens the other flavours, softens bitterness and makes the dish taste more of itself.

cards.front: When do you salt a braise or a soup?
cards.back: Early and lightly, so the salt works into the meat and vegetables, then adjust at the end.

cards.front: Why is a reduction salted late?
cards.back: Reduction drives off water but leaves the salt behind, so a sauce seasoned at the start grows saltier as it reduces.

cards.front: How does acid work as a seasoning?
cards.back: A few drops of lemon or vinegar lift a rich butter sauce or a long-cooked gumbo, so it tastes brighter rather than sour.

cards.front: How does Creole cooking use cayenne, pepper and hot sauce?
cards.back: As seasonings that warm and round a dish, in balance with its salt, acid and richness, never as a dare.

cards.front: Why use white pepper in a pale sauce?
cards.back: It gives pepper's warmth without dark specks, so a white sauce stays clean to the eye.

cards.front: Why taste sauce, protein and garnish together?
cards.back: The guest eats them together: a sauce that seems strong alone may be right over plain fish, and salty parts add up.

cards.front: How do you correct a sauce that is too salty?
cards.back: Dilute it with more of the unsalted base, stock, cream or the main ingredient; acid or fat softens the edge, but nothing removes salt.

cards.front: A sauce tastes flat. What do you reach for first?
cards.back: Salt first, then a drop of acid: a flat sauce is usually under-seasoned rather than missing an ingredient.

cards.front: What corrects a dish that is too sharp, too sweet or too hot?
cards.back: Too sharp: butter, cream or a pinch of sugar. Too sweet: acid and salt. Too hot: more of the base, or fat, cream or starch.

cards.front: How do you describe the Creole spice on the breakfast hanger steak?
cards.back: Warm and savoury rather than fiery, in the style of the house's own Creole spice; the blend is not printed, so spice questions go to the kitchen.

questions.q: You have tasted a sauce with a spoon. What do you do before tasting it again?
distractors: Wipe the spoon on a side towel
Rinse the spoon in the sauce
Dip the same spoon straight back
questions.why: A used spoon carries the taster's mouth back into the food; the Food Code allows a utensil one taste only.

questions.q: Why is a sauce that will be reduced salted only at the end?
distractors: Salt stops a sauce from reducing
Salt boils away with the water
Salt turns bitter when heated
questions.why: Water evaporates but salt stays, so a sauce seasoned fully at the start grows saltier as it reduces.

questions.q: When should a braise first be salted?
questions.answer: Early and lightly, adjusted at the end
distractors: Only at the table, by the guest
Heavily at the start, and never again
Only after it has been reduced
questions.why: Early salt works into the meat and vegetables through the long cook; a final taste corrects what the pot needs.

questions.q: A rich butter sauce tastes heavy and dull. What small addition lifts it?
questions.answer: A few drops of lemon juice
distractors: A spoonful of white sugar
A pinch of plain flour
A knob of melted butter
questions.why: Acid cuts through fat and brightens the other flavours; a few drops make a rich sauce taste lighter without tasting sour.

questions.q: A soup is too salty. What is the honest fix?
questions.answer: Dilute it with more unsalted base
distractors: Add a raw potato to absorb the salt
Boil it hard to drive off the salt
Add sugar until the salt disappears
questions.why: Salt cannot be taken out: a potato absorbs only a little salty liquid and boiling concentrates salt, so more base lowers it.

questions.q: A sauce tastes flat. Which correction comes first?
questions.answer: Salt, then a drop of acid
distractors: A pinch of sugar, then butter
More cayenne and hot sauce
A spoonful of flour
questions.why: Flatness is usually a want of salt; acid then brightens it, while sugar, heat or flour only mask or thicken.

questions.q: Why might a cook choose white pepper over black for a béchamel?
distractors: It has no heat at all
It thickens the sauce
It keeps the sauce from splitting
questions.why: White pepper brings pepper's warmth without black flecks, so a white sauce looks as clean as it tastes.

questions.q: Why does a chef taste the sauce, the protein and the garnish in one forkful?
distractors: It saves clean spoons
Sauces cannot be tasted alone
It cools the food faster
questions.why: Seasoning is judged as the guest meets it: a strong sauce may be right over plain fish, and salty parts add up.

questions.q: How should a server describe the Creole spice on the breakfast hanger steak?
questions.answer: Warm and savoury rather than fiery
distractors: Fiery, with a slow-building burn
Sweet and smoky, like a barbecue rub
Sharp and sour, like a vinegar hot sauce
questions.why: The house describes its Creole spice as warm and savoury rather than fiery; the blend is not printed, so a question about a particular spice or the heat goes to the kitchen.

steps.title: Set a sauce station
steps.prompt: Put the stages of setting a sauce station before service in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Read the book for the covers booked and when the rush will land
Count what is left from yesterday against the par and write the prep list
With the prep list written, anchor the board on a damp cloth, with knives, dry side towels and a scrap bowl at hand
Cut the shallots ciselé and pick the herbs from their stems
Reduce vinegar with shallot and tarragon for the béarnaise, then strain it
With service minutes away, set the clarified butter warm, never hot, beside the stocks held hot at the back of the stove
steps.distractor: Peel and cut the shallots as each ticket comes in, so they stay fresh
steps.why: The book sets the par and the par sets the prep list. The board is anchored before any knife work, the shallot and herbs are cut before they go into the reduction, and the clarified butter is set warm last, so it is never held hot for long.

steps.title: Make a white chicken stock
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a white chicken stock in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Cut the carcasses, necks, wings and feet to fit the pot and rinse them well
Cover them with cold water by about 5 cm (2 inches)
Bring it slowly to a bare simmer, skimming the scum as it rises
Add the onion, celery, leek, bouquet garni and peppercorns once the first scum is off
Simmer for 3 to 5 hours, unsalted, topping up with cold water if the bones show
Ladle the stock through a chinois lined with muslin, never tipping the pot
Cool it fast, then lift off the fat once it has set
steps.distractor: Roast the bones to a deep brown before they go into the pot
steps.why: Cold water and a slow rise bring the scum up where it can be skimmed, and the vegetables follow once it is off. A bare, unsalted simmer and a gentle ladle keep the stock pale and clear.

steps.title: Make a brown stock
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a classical brown veal stock in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Roast the veal bones in one layer at about 220°C (428°F) until deep mahogany
Add the onion, carrot and celery for the last 20 to 30 minutes of roasting
Smear on tomato purée and roast until it turns from red to rust
Lift everything into the stockpot, pour the fat from the tray, then deglaze the tray into the pot with a little water or wine
Cover with cold water, bring it up slowly and skim the foam
Hold a bare simmer for 8 to 12 hours, skimming fat and foam through the day
Add parsley stalks, thyme, bay and peppercorns for the last hour
Strain through a chinois without pressing, cool it quickly and lift off the set fat
steps.distractor: Salt the water well so the stock tastes finished
steps.why: Colour comes first, from bones, vegetables and tomato browned in turn, and the tray is deglazed so its juices reach the pot. Then comes a long, bare simmer with no salt, because a salted stock cannot be reduced.

steps.title: Make a fish fumet
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a fumet de poisson in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Pull out the gills and chop the frames of lean white fish
Soak the bones in cold water until it runs clear, then drain them
Sweat onion, celery and mushroom trim in butter with the drained bones on top, covered, for about 5 minutes without colour
Pour in dry white wine and let it bubble for a minute
Add cold water just to cover, bring it to a bare simmer and skim
Add the herbs and white peppercorns and simmer for 20 to 30 minutes, no longer
Ladle it through muslin without pressing the bones, then cool it quickly
steps.distractor: Simmer it for 4 hours to draw out all the gelatine
steps.why: Clean, bloodless bones are sweated in butter for a rounder taste, and the wine bubbles before the water goes in. The simmer stops at half an hour, because fish bones give up bitterness after that.

steps.title: Make a court-bouillon and poach in it
steps.prompt: Put the stages of making a court-bouillon and poaching a whole fish in it in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Bring water, white wine, sliced onion, carrot and celery, a bouquet garni and salt to the boil
Simmer for 20 to 30 minutes, adding the peppercorns for the last 10 only
Strain it and let it cool
Lay the whole fish in the cool court-bouillon
Bring it up gently until the surface barely trembles
Hold it just below a simmer, about 75 to 85°C (167 to 185°F), until the fish is cooked through
Lift the fish out gently so it stays whole
steps.distractor: Lower the whole fish into the court-bouillon at a rolling boil
steps.why: The broth simmers first so it has flavour to give, with the peppercorns late so they do not turn bitter. A whole fish starts cool and comes up gently, and once it is in, the liquid never boils.

steps.title: Clarify a consommé with a raft
steps.prompt: Put the stages of clarifying a consommé with a raft in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Mix the raft of lean minced meat, egg whites, chopped mirepoix and tomato in a tall pot with the cold, fat-free stock
Heat it slowly, stirring and scraping the bottom
Stop stirring once the raft begins to gather and the liquid turns cloudy, around 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F)
Open a vent near the edge of the raft with a ladle
Hold the barest simmer through the vent for an hour to an hour and a half
Ladle the consommé out through the vent and pass it through damp muslin
Blot off the last of the fat with kitchen paper and season lightly
steps.distractor: Stir the raft back through the stock as it simmers, for more flavour
steps.why: Raft and stock heat together from cold, so the proteins set slowly and catch what clouds the stock. Once the raft gathers it is left alone, the vent lets the stock baste it, and gentle ladling keeps it whole.
